title: Greetings
description: Hello and goodbye across the day, with formality notes.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: Korean greetings are strongly tied to formality and respect. Learn the polite set first.

steps.title: Form vs. familiarity
steps.body: Use 존댓말 (polite speech) with strangers and elders. Casual speech is for close friends.
bullets: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose polite hello.
안녕히 가세요 when the other person is leaving.
안녕히 계세요 when you are leaving.
안녕 is casual hi/bye.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean greeting with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, how are you?":
steps.explanation: A warm, time-appropriate greeting — the foundation of any first impression.

steps.title: Listen · polite hello
steps.prompt: You hear this greeting. What does it mean?
Reply politely and return the question:
steps.explanation: "네, 잘 지내요. 어떻게 지내세요?" answers politely and returns the question in the honorific -세요 form. "안녕히 가세요" is a goodbye.

steps.title: Check · polite
steps.prompt: Which is the standard polite hello?
steps.explanation: 안녕하세요 is the safe polite greeting.

steps.title: Check · formality
steps.prompt: You meet your friend’s parent for the first time. Best choice?
steps.explanation: Polite speech is required with elders and strangers.

steps.title: Check · good night
steps.prompt: You’re heading to bed. You say…
steps.explanation: 잘 자요 is the polite good night.

title: Please & thank you
description: Politeness formulas that open every exchange.

steps.title: Small words, big difference
steps.body: Korean interactions expect 주세요 and 감사합니다.

steps.title: Please & thanks
steps.body: 주세요 is the everyday “please (give me).” 감사합니다 is polite thanks.
bullets: 감사합니다 / 고맙습니다 = thank you.
천만에요 / 아니에요 = you’re welcome.
죄송합니다 = I’m sorry (formal).
미안해요 is softer.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean polite phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A coffee, please.":
steps.explanation: Combining a request with "please" — the cornerstone of polite interaction.

steps.title: Listen · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says 감사합니다. A common reply is…

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Here you go, your coffee is ready. That's 3,000 won.
steps.prompt: Thank him as you pay:
steps.explanation: "감사합니다" is the polite thank-you. "천만에요" (you're welcome) is what the clerk might say back.

steps.title: Check · shop
steps.prompt: How do you say “please” when ordering?
steps.explanation: 주세요 is the standard request ending.

steps.title: Check · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says 감사합니다. A common reply is…
steps.explanation: 천만에요 means “you’re welcome.”

title: Numbers 1–10
description: Count clearly for prices, times, and quantities.

steps.title: Count slowly
steps.body: Korean has two number systems: native and Sino-Korean. Both are essential.

steps.title: Two systems
steps.body: Native Korean numbers (하나, 둘…) are used for small quantities and age. Sino-Korean (일, 이…) for money, dates, phone numbers.
bullets: 하나, 둘, 셋… (native)
일, 이, 삼… (Sino)
Beginners need both.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean number with its numeral:
Arrange the stones to say: "Two coffees, please.":
steps.explanation: Numbers in context — the essential combination for real-world transactions.

steps.title: Listen · age
steps.prompt: Someone says this. How old are they?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: How many tickets shall I give you?
steps.prompt: Ask for two tickets:
steps.explanation: "두 장 주세요" uses the counter 장 for tickets with the native number 두. "만오천 원입니다" is the price the clerk would quote.

steps.title: Check · native seven
steps.prompt: What is native Korean “seven”?
steps.explanation: 일곱 is native Korean seven.

steps.title: Check · phrase
steps.prompt: “커피 둘” means…
steps.explanation: 둘 means two (native).

steps.title: Check · age
steps.prompt: How do Koreans say “I am twenty years old”?
steps.explanation: Age often uses native numbers + 살.

title: Introduce yourself
description: Name, origin, and a simple nice-to-meet-you.

steps.title: First contact
steps.body: A short self-introduction is enough: name, origin, and a polite close.

steps.title: 만나서 반갑습니다
steps.body: This is the standard polite “nice to meet you.”

steps.prompt: Match each Korean introduction phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, my name is Alex.":
steps.explanation: Your origin in one clear sentence — the natural follow-up to sharing your name.

steps.title: Listen · origin
steps.prompt: What does this person say?

steps.partnerSays: 만나서 반갑습니다. 제 이름은 레아입니다. 어디에서 오셨어요?
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: mannaseo bangapseumnida. je ireumeun Rea-imnida. eodieseo osyeosseoyo?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Nice to meet you. My name is Lea. Where are you from?
steps.prompt: Say where you're from and return the question:
steps.explanation: "미국에서 왔습니다. 레아 씨는요?" answers her question and returns it using her name + 씨, which is more natural than 당신.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: “제 이름은 샘입니다” means…
steps.explanation: 제 이름은 …입니다 = my name is…

steps.title: Check · origin
steps.prompt: Best line for “I come from Belgium”?
steps.explanation: …에서 왔습니다 expresses origin.

title: Colors & simple descriptions
description: Name colors and describe everyday objects.

steps.title: Painting with words
steps.body: Korean colors are often descriptive verbs or nouns + 색.

steps.title: Color forms
steps.body: Many colors end in 색 (color) or use 이다.
bullets: 빨간색 = red
파란색 = blue
검은색 = black

steps.prompt: Match each Korean color with its English name:
Arrange the stones to say: "a blue dress":
steps.explanation: Color + polite form — everything needed to express a preference in any shop.

steps.title: Listen · color
steps.prompt: You hear “빨간색 치마”. What is being described?
Ask for the red one:
steps.explanation: "빨간색으로 주세요" (the red one, please) answers the question about color politely.

steps.title: Check · color
steps.prompt: How do you say “red”?
steps.explanation: 빨간색 = red.

steps.title: Check · black
steps.prompt: What is “black” in Korean?
steps.explanation: 검은색 = black.

title: At the café
description: Order drinks and ask for the bill with confidence.

steps.title: A quiet table
steps.body: A handful of drink words plus a polite request phrase is enough to order confidently anywhere.

steps.title: Café culture
steps.body: Ask for the bill — servers rarely bring it unsolicited. Tipping customs vary by country.
bullets: For here or to go? — learn both forms.
A jug of tap water is often free — always worth asking.

phrases.source: I would like a coffee, please.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "One coffee, please.":
steps.explanation: A polite order that works in any café — commit it to memory for the first sip.

steps.title: Listen · bill
steps.prompt: How do you ask for the bill?
Order a coffee politely:
steps.explanation: "커피 한 잔 주세요" (one cup of coffee, please) is the natural way to order.

steps.title: Check · bill
steps.prompt: How do you say "the bill" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 계산서 is the bill/check.

steps.title: Check · to go
steps.prompt: How do you say "to go" when ordering?
steps.explanation: 포장 means packaging/to go.

title: At the market
description: Fruit, quantities, and polite requests at a stall.

steps.title: Market pace
steps.body: Markets reward clear numbers and a polite request. Pointing plus a word works — language makes it smoother.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Three apples, please.":
steps.explanation: Quantity, item, price question — the complete phrase for any market stall.

steps.title: Listen · price
steps.prompt: How do you ask "How much is it?"
Ask for three apples and the price:
steps.explanation: "사과 세 개 주세요. 얼마예요?" adds to your order and asks the price.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you ask the price in Korean?
steps.explanation: 얼마예요? = How much is it? A core shopping question.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Best for "three apples, please"?
steps.explanation: 사과 세 개 주세요 directly matches the request.

title: Small talk & weather
description: Light conversation beyond hello.

steps.title: Beyond hello
steps.body: Weather and weekend questions are safe bridges after greetings. A comment on the sun or rain opens doors.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Nice weather today.":
steps.explanation: A light observation that opens the door to warm, easy conversation.

steps.title: Listen · rain
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's raining"?
Agree and keep the chat going:
steps.explanation: Agreeing and asking about the weekend keeps the small talk flowing.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's raining" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 비가 와요 = rain comes = It's raining. 비 is rain, 와요 is comes.

steps.title: Check · weekend
steps.prompt: How do you ask "How was your weekend?"
steps.explanation: 주말 어떻게 보내셨어요? uses the honorific past form 보내셨어요?

title: At the restaurant
description: Ordering a meal and dietary needs.

steps.title: From table to bill
steps.body: Ordering follows a clear rhythm: being seated, choosing, ordering, and asking for the bill.

steps.title: Cultural notes
steps.body: Learn the word for "Enjoy your meal!" and the dietary vocabulary relevant to your needs.
bullets: Vegetarian and vegan options are now widely available.
Stating allergies early is always wise.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "We have two people.":
steps.explanation: The natural, confident way to place an order with any server.

steps.title: Listen · recommendation
steps.prompt: How do you ask "What do you recommend?"
Order the fish:
steps.explanation: "생선으로 주세요" (the fish, please) uses 으로 to indicate choice.

steps.title: Check · menu
steps.prompt: 메뉴 in Korean refers to…
options: The full list of every dish
steps.explanation: 메뉴 is the menu with all available dishes.

steps.title: Check · vegetarian
steps.prompt: How does a person say "I'm vegetarian" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 저는 채식주의자예요 = I am a vegetarian.

title: Talking about plans
description: Express what you're going to do.

steps.title: The near future
steps.body: Each language has a simple structure to talk about upcoming plans.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Learn the future/plan marker for your language.
bullets: Haitian Creole: pral + verb (no conjugation)
Korean: ~(으)ㄹ 거예요
Chinese: 打算 + verb or 要 + verb

phrases.source: What are you going to do this weekend?
I'm going to visit my parents.
We're going to watch a film.
She's going to travel to Busan.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I'm going to visit my parents.":
steps.targetTranslation: I'm going to visit my parents.
steps.explanation: Future marker + plan — two building blocks for any upcoming arrangement.

steps.title: Listen · structure
steps.prompt: Which uses the Korean future correctly?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: What are you going to do this weekend?
steps.prompt: Say you're going to visit your parents:
steps.explanation: "갈 거예요" uses the future form ~(으)ㄹ 거예요 to express a plan.

steps.title: Check · structure
steps.prompt: Which correctly uses ~(으)ㄹ 거예요?
steps.explanation: 먹을 거예요 = will eat / going to eat. ~(으)ㄹ 거예요 is the future intention form.

steps.title: Check · translate
steps.prompt: How do you say "We will travel" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 여행할 거예요 = will travel (future intention form).

title: Simple directions
description: Left, right, straight — and asking where something is.

steps.title: Finding your way
steps.body: Combine "where is…?" with a few direction words for short walks in a new city.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Go straight, then turn left.":
steps.explanation: Left, right, and straight — three words that will get you anywhere in the city.

steps.title: Listen · where
steps.prompt: How do you ask "Where is the station?"

steps.partnerSays: 쭉 가다가 왼쪽으로 가세요. 약국 맞은편이에요.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Go straight then turn left. It's across from the pharmacy.
steps.prompt: Ask whether it's far:
steps.explanation: "멀어요?" is the natural follow-up after getting directions.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "straight ahead" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 직진 means straight ahead; 왼쪽/오른쪽으로 are left/right.

steps.title: Check · ask
steps.prompt: How do you ask where the station is?
steps.explanation: …이/가 어디예요? = Where is…? The essential navigation question.

title: Travel phrases
description: Tickets, platforms, and delays.

steps.title: On the move
steps.body: Stations repeat the same patterns: destination, platform, delay. Learn them once.

phrases.target: 서울 가는 표 한 장 주세요.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "One ticket to Seoul, please.":
steps.targetSentence: 서울 가는 표 한 장 주세요.
steps.explanation: A direct question that instantly tells you if you're running on schedule.

steps.title: Listen · delay
steps.prompt: How do you say "The train is delayed"?
Ask if the train is running late:
options: 서울 가는 표 한 장 주세요.
steps.explanation: "기차가 연착인가요?" asks about a delay.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "a ticket" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 표 (pyo) is the most common word for a train/bus ticket.

steps.title: Check · delay
steps.prompt: How do you say "delayed" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 연착 means late/delayed; 정시에 means on time.

title: At the hotel
description: Check-in lines and simple room requests.

steps.title: Front desk
steps.body: Reservation, nights, and room type cover most check-ins.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have a reservation.":
steps.explanation: A short statement that confirms your booking and sets check-in in motion.

steps.title: Listen · breakfast
steps.prompt: How do you ask "Is breakfast included?"
Confirm and ask about breakfast:
steps.explanation: "네. 조식이 포함돼 있나요?" confirms and asks a key check-in question.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you say "I have a reservation" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 예약이 있어요 = I have a reservation. 예약 = reservation.

steps.title: Check · checkout
steps.prompt: How do you ask what time checkout is?
steps.explanation: 체크아웃이 몇 시예요? = What time is checkout?

title: Getting around town
description: Buses, metro, taxis, and buying tickets.

steps.title: Moving through the city
steps.body: Most cities run on a mix of metro, bus, and taxi. A few words cover most fare questions.

phrases.source: Does this bus go to downtown?
I'm getting off at the next stop.
Can you call me a taxi?

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Does this bus go downtown?":
steps.explanation: The phrase that ends any bus or metro journey gracefully.

steps.title: Listen · getting off
steps.prompt: How do you say "I'm getting off at the next stop"?
Say you're getting off at the next stop:
steps.explanation: "다음 정류장에서 내릴게요" tells the driver where you want to get off.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: 일일 교통카드 usually refers to…
steps.explanation: 일일 교통카드 is a day pass; 단일 승차권 is a single fare.

steps.title: Check · getting off
steps.prompt: How do you say "I'm getting off here"?
steps.explanation: 내리다 means to get off; 타다 means to get on.

title: Pharmacy & feeling unwell
description: Describe symptoms and get help at a pharmacy.

steps.title: Getting help
steps.body: Pharmacies are trained to advise on minor issues before you need a doctor.

steps.title: Pain pattern
steps.body: Each language has a go-to pattern for expressing physical pain.
bullets: Haitian Creole: mwen gen yon doulè nan… (I have pain in…)
Korean: …이/가 아파요 (… hurts)
Chinese: …疼 / 我…疼 (… hurts)

phrases.source: Do you have something for a sore throat?

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "My head hurts.":
steps.explanation: Describing the most common ache — clear and calm gets you the right remedy.

steps.title: Listen · stomach
steps.prompt: Which phrase means "I have a stomach ache"?
Say no and ask for something for your throat:
steps.explanation: "아니요. 목에 좋은 약 있나요?" answers and asks for an over-the-counter remedy.

steps.title: Check · pattern
steps.prompt: How do you say "My head hurts" in Korean?
steps.explanation: …이/가 아파요 = … hurts. 머리가 아파요 = My head hurts.

steps.title: Check · emergency
steps.prompt: Which phrase calls for urgent help?
steps.explanation: 도와주세요! = Please help me! The standard call for help in Korean.

title: Telling time
description: Ask for and give the time, on the hour and beyond.

steps.title: What time is it?
steps.body: Each language has a key question for asking the time and a standard way to give it.

steps.title: Minute expressions
steps.body: Learn the fixed time expressions for each language.
bullets: Haitian Creole: è (o'clock), e mwatye (half past), e ka (quarter past)
Korean: 시 (hour), 분 (minute), 반 (half)
Chinese: 点 (hour), 分 (minute), 半 (half)

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "It's half past seven.":
steps.explanation: Hour + "half" — the most common time expression in everyday conversation.

steps.title: Listen · half past
steps.prompt: How do you say "half past seven"?
Thank her and say when your train leaves:
steps.explanation: "감사합니다. 기차는 세 시에 출발해요" thanks her and states the departure time.

steps.title: Check · 반
steps.prompt: "… 시 반" in Korean means…
steps.explanation: 반 means half, so 일곱 시 반 = seven thirty = half past seven.

steps.title: Check · noon
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's noon" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 정오 is noon; 자정 is midnight.

title: Days, months & dates
description: The calendar and how to say a date.

steps.title: Calendar basics
steps.body: Learning days and months opens up conversations about plans, birthdays, and appointments.

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "My birthday is May 1st.":
steps.explanation: A date in full — once you know the pattern, every date falls into place.

steps.title: Listen · day
steps.prompt: How do you say "Today is Monday"?
Say it's Wednesday:
steps.explanation: "오늘은 수요일이에요" answers with the day. 이에요 is the polite copula.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Which day comes right after 수요일 (Wednesday)?
steps.explanation: The order: 월요일, 화요일, 수요일, 목요일, 금요일, 토요일, 일요일.

steps.title: Check · months
steps.prompt: How do you say "May" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 5월 = 오월 (five-month). Korean months use Sino-Korean numbers + 월.

title: Talking about family
description: Name family members and describe relationships.

steps.title: Who's who
steps.body: Family vocabulary combines with "to have" and possessives for quick descriptions.

steps.title: Age-relative terms
steps.body: Korean and Chinese use different words depending on whether a sibling is older or younger.
bullets: Korean: 오빠/형 (older brother from woman/man's perspective), 언니/누나 (older sister), 남동생/여동생 (younger siblings)
Chinese: 哥哥/弟弟 (older/younger brother), 姐姐/妹妹 (older/younger sister)
Haitian Creole: frè (brother), sè (sister) — no age distinction

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I have two younger brothers.":
steps.explanation: A warm, simple statement that naturally invites the other person to share too.

steps.title: Listen · possessive
steps.prompt: How do you say "my older sister (from a woman's perspective)"?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Nice to meet you. Do you have siblings?
steps.prompt: Say you have two brothers:
steps.explanation: "네, 남동생이 두 명 있어요" answers with the counter 명 for people.

steps.title: Check · sibling terms
steps.prompt: An older sister, from a woman's perspective, is called…
steps.explanation: 언니 = older sister (said by a woman). 누나 = older sister (said by a man). 오빠 = older brother (by woman). 형 = older brother (by man).

steps.title: Check · plural
steps.prompt: How do you say "my parents" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 부모님 = parents (父母 + honorific 님). 제 부모님 = my parents.

title: Shopping for clothes
description: Sizes, trying things on, and asking about price.

steps.title: Trying it on
steps.body: Clothes shopping mixes size, color, and a few polite requests to try things on or ask for a different size.

phrases.source: Do you have this in a size M?
Do you have a bigger size?

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Do you have this in size M?":
steps.targetTranslation: Do you have this in size M?
steps.explanation: The one question that keeps a shopping trip moving in the right direction.

steps.title: Listen · size
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's too small"?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Of course. The fitting room is over there.
steps.prompt: After trying it on, say it's too small and ask for a bigger size:
options: 너무 작아요. 더 큰 사이즈 있나요?
steps.correctAnswer: 너무 작아요. 더 큰 사이즈 있나요?
steps.explanation: "너무 작아요. 더 큰 사이즈 있나요?" describes the problem and asks for the next size.

steps.title: Check · size
steps.prompt: How do you ask "do you have this in size M?"
steps.explanation: 사이즈 means size; M 사이즈 = size M.

steps.title: Check · too small
steps.prompt: How do you say "It's too small" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 너무 작아요 = too small; 너무 커요 = too big.

title: Grammar: articles & markers
description: How these languages mark nouns and structure sentences.

steps.title: Nouns and their markers
steps.body: Haitian Creole, Korean, and Chinese each handle definiteness and nouns very differently from European languages.

steps.title: Key differences
steps.body: No language in this group has gender like French or Spanish.
bullets: Haitian Creole: definite article la/a/an comes AFTER the noun; no gender
Korean: no articles; topic (은/는) and subject (이/가) markers do important grammar work
Chinese: no articles, no gender; measure words are required between numbers and nouns

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I read a book.":
steps.explanation: A compact phrase that puts the article or gender rule into immediate practice.

steps.title: Listen · particles
steps.prompt: Which particle marks the object of a verb?
steps.explanation: 을/를 marks the object: 책을 (book [object]).

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: In Korean, which particle is used with '책' (book) as a subject?
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: hangugeo eseo chaek eun eotteon josa reul sseoyo?
steps.prompt: Answer correctly:
steps.explanation: 이/가 marks the subject. 을/를 marks the object. 은/는 marks the topic. Korean has no articles or gender.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: Which particle marks the topic of a sentence in Korean?
steps.explanation: 은/는 marks the topic (known information or contrast). 이/가 marks the subject (new information).

steps.title: Check · gender
steps.prompt: Which statement about Korean gender is correct?
options: Changes verb endings based on noun gender
steps.explanation: Korean has no grammatical gender. Nouns are simply nouns.

steps.title: Check · articles
steps.prompt: Korean uses _____ to mark definiteness and topics.
steps.explanation: Korean uses particles (조사) attached after nouns to show grammatical function.

title: To be & to have
description: The core verbs — and how they differ across languages.

steps.title: Workhorses
steps.body: The concepts of "to be" and "to have" exist in all three languages but work quite differently.

steps.title: 이다 / 있다 — to be / to exist

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I am tired.":
steps.explanation: Two core verbs in a single sentence — a powerful combination to internalize.

steps.title: Listen · identity
steps.prompt: How do you say "She is Korean"?
Say you're tired and hungry:
steps.explanation: Tiredness: 피곤하다. Hunger: 배가 고프다. Both are adjective predicates in Korean.

steps.title: Check · 이다
steps.prompt: How do you say "I am a student" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 이에요/예요 is the polite present form of 이다 (to be): 학생이에요 = am a student.

steps.title: Check · 있다
steps.prompt: "예약이 있어요" means…
steps.explanation: 있어요 = there is / to have. 예약이 있어요 = (there is a reservation) = I have a reservation.

steps.title: Check · hungry
steps.prompt: How do you say "they are hungry" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 배가 고파요 = stomach is empty = to be hungry. This is an adjective predicate.

title: Verbs & patterns
description: How verbs work in these three languages.

steps.title: Verb patterns
steps.body: Haitian Creole verbs don't conjugate at all — the biggest advantage for learners! Korean and Chinese also avoid the complexity of European conjugation.

steps.title: Verb patterns compared
steps.body: These languages express tense and aspect very differently.
bullets: Haitian Creole: verbs never change. Aspect markers (ap, te, pral) are added.
Korean: verbs conjugate for politeness and tense, but not for person or gender.
Chinese: verbs never change. Tense is shown by time words and aspect particles (了, 过, 着).

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I speak a little Korean.":
steps.explanation: The verb pattern in action — master this form and unlock a whole verb family.

steps.title: Listen · tense
steps.prompt: Which form is the past tense "I worked"?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Do you know how to speak Korean?
steps.prompt: Say yes, you speak a little Korean:
steps.explanation: 해요 is the informal polite form of 하다 (to do/speak). 합니다 is the formal polite form.

steps.title: Check · politeness
steps.prompt: Korean verbs change based on…
steps.explanation: Korean verbs conjugate for politeness (formal: -ㅂ니다, informal polite: -아/어요) but NOT for grammatical person.

steps.title: Check · progressive
steps.prompt: Which form means "is eating" (in progress)?
steps.explanation: 먹고 있어요 = verb stem + 고 있다 is the progressive form in Korean.

title: Adjectives & descriptions
description: How descriptive words work in these languages.

steps.title: Describing things
steps.body: None of these three languages has the gender agreement of European Romance languages, which simplifies adjective use significantly.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body: Adjectives work simply in these languages.
bullets: Haitian Creole: adjectives never change for gender or number
Korean: adjectives conjugate like verbs (for tense/politeness) but not for gender/number of the noun
Chinese: adjectives don't change form; predicative adjectives usually take 很 (hěn)

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "She is small.":
steps.explanation: Agreement at work: the adjective shifts to match the noun it describes.

steps.title: Listen · adjective
steps.prompt: Which form means "tall" in Korean?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: My brother is tall. What about your older sister?
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: je oppaneun kiga keoyo. eonni neunyo?
steps.prompt: Describe your sister the same way:
steps.explanation: Korean adjectives don't agree for gender. 키가 커요 works for anyone.

steps.title: Check · no gender
steps.prompt: In Korean, how does "tall" (커요) change for a woman?
steps.explanation: Korean adjectives don't change for gender. 커요 works for men, women, and things.

steps.title: Check · verb-like
steps.prompt: Korean adjectives conjugate like…
steps.explanation: Korean adjectives (형용사) conjugate like verbs for tense and speech level: 커요 (polite), 크다 (dictionary form).

title: Saying no
description: Turn any sentence negative with simple patterns.

steps.title: Negation patterns
steps.body: Each language has a characteristic way to negate a verb. Learn the pattern, apply it everywhere.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Negation is relatively straightforward in all three languages.
bullets: Haitian Creole: pa before the verb
Korean: 안 before verb/adjective, or -지 않다 after the stem
Chinese: 不 (bù) for general negation, 没 (méi) for past/existence

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I don't like coffee.":
steps.explanation: The negation pattern in its simplest form — learn it once, use it everywhere.

steps.title: Listen · 안
steps.prompt: Which correctly negates "I like coffee"?
Say no, you don't like coffee:
steps.explanation: 안 is placed directly before the verb/adjective to negate it: 안 좋아해요.

steps.title: Check · 안 vs. 못
steps.prompt: What is the difference between 안 and 못?
options: 안 is past; 못 is present
steps.explanation: 안 = don't / doesn't (choice). 못 = can't (inability): 안 가요 (I don't go), 못 가요 (I can't go).

steps.title: Check · placement
steps.prompt: Where does 안 go in a Korean sentence?
steps.explanation: 안 goes directly before the verb or adjective it negates: 안 좋아해요, 안 먹어요.

title: Asking questions
description: Question words and patterns.

steps.title: Asking around
steps.body: Each language has its own set of question words and question-formation patterns.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Yes/no and information questions each have their own structure.
bullets: Haitian Creole: eske at the start for yes/no; question word replaces the unknown element
Korean: question words in place of what they ask; -요? at the end for polite questions
Chinese: question words in place of what they ask; 吗 (ma) at the end for yes/no questions

steps.prompt: Match each Korean word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Where do you live?":
steps.explanation: A well-formed question using the key structure — polite, clear, and natural.

steps.title: Listen · why
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Korean?
Ask where she lives:
steps.explanation: Question words in Korean go in the position of what they're asking about: 어디에 살아요?

steps.title: Check · word meaning
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Korean?
steps.explanation: 왜 = why; it pairs with 왜냐하면 / 때문에 (because) in the answer.

steps.title: Check · yes/no question
steps.prompt: Korean yes/no questions end with…
steps.explanation: Korean yes/no questions use rising intonation + -요? (polite): 영어 해요? (Do you speak English?)
